title: Challenge Accepted: Improving Our Feedback
author: Ben Zulauf Source: benzulauf.substack.com
summary: Part 3 of Ben Zulauf's Challenge Accepted series on teacher evaluation, this piece argues that the root failure of evaluation is evaluators' lack of deep instructional knowledge — they cannot recognize or diagnose effective teaching moves they've never been trained to see. Most principal preparation programs cover law, finance, and organizational theory but not learning science; what is taught often contradicts the research (e.g., teaching standards in isolation rather than building connected knowledge). The proposed solution starts with building evaluators' knowledge through rigorous, calendar-scheduled professional development — not vaguely acknowledging that PD is needed, but committing to specific dates. Because building this knowledge means unlearning deeply held beliefs, evaluators will experience significant cognitive dissonance; planning for that emotional arc well in advance is as essential as a teacher scaffolding students through difficult content. Beyond knowledge, a sequential instructional framework is needed: the Danielson Framework's domain structure leaves evaluators without clear guidance on where to start, producing inconsistent emphasis across schools. Part 4 will introduce a specific sequential framework tied to how learning actually unfolds.
points: The root of poor teacher evaluation is not ill intent but evaluators' lack of instructional knowledge — they cannot see teaching moves they've never been trained to recognize, just as a football fan can't spot a false start without knowing the rule.

Principal preparation programs typically omit the science of learning; what is taught often contradicts research (e.g., teaching and assessing standards in isolation rather than building connected knowledge).

Building evaluators' knowledge requires not just acknowledging the need for PD but committing to specific calendar dates — vague intentions don't change practice; Dylan Wiliam's 'opportunity cost is the single most important concept in educational improvement' applies to professional development design as much as lesson design.

Unlearning deeply held instructional beliefs produces cognitive dissonance; districts must plan for this emotional arc as carefully as a teacher plans scaffolding — the robust PD plan must be created well in advance to support staff through that process.

The Danielson Framework leaves evaluators without clear sequencing of where to start, producing inconsistent emphasis; a sequential framework tied to how learning unfolds is the proposed structural fix.
quotes: How can we expect evaluations to consistently produce better results when the preparation programs do not provide people with the knowledge needed to evaluate?

If teachers do not come out of their preparation programs with a solid understanding of teaching and learning, then the onus is on the district to provide professional development. The same thing is true for administrators.

Knowing that we lack a nuanced understanding, we need to ensure that we have a rigorous professional development calendar that helps evaluators understand the intentional teacher moves that have the biggest impact on learning.

Dylan Wiliam has stated that 'opportunity cost is the single most important concept in educational improvement.' Each of these practices has a place, and they can be used in conjunction with one another, but we need to understand the cost of selecting one strategy over another.

The staff in your district may experience the same cognitive dissonance, so the robust PD plan that you implement will need to be created well in advance of executing it so that you're readily available to support people as they experience the cognitive dissonance that they will likely feel.
